questions: What happens if both operations are applicable at the same time for a given i?
Can we apply the operations simultaneously or must they be applied sequentially?
Is it allowed to perform operations on indices that have already been modified by previous operations?
Does "any number of times" include performing the same operation multiple times on overlapping indices?
Are the characters in the string S required to be exactly 'A', 'R', 'C' or can they be any uppercase English letters?
What is the initial state of the sequence A before any operations are performed?
If N=3 and we perform an operation, do the wraparound indices correctly update A_1 and A_2 when i=2?
When checking for existence of a good string, do we need to find at least one specific string S or prove that any valid construction works?
answers: Not specified; if both operations are simultaneously applicable for some i, either may be chosen (they don't conflict, since both only ever set A_i and A_{i+1} to 1).
Operations are applied sequentially, one at a time, not simultaneously.
Yes, operations may be performed on indices already affected by earlier operations.
Yes, 'any number of times' allows repeating operations on the same or overlapping indices.
S is uppercase-letter content used to match the 'A','R','C' pattern at specific positions; beyond that its alphabet isn't further restricted here.
The initial state of A is exactly the input sequence given.
Yes, the given wraparound definitions (S_{N+1}=S_1, A_{N+1}=A_1) correctly handle the case N=3, i=2.
We need to determine whether there exists at least one good string S, as stated -- not prove a specific construction.
inline_prompts: You are given a positive integer N and a sequence A=(A_1,A_2,\dots,A_N) of length N, consisting of 0 and 1. We call a string S of length N, consisting only of uppercase English letters, a good string if it is possible to perform the following operation any number of times (possibly zero). Here, S_i (1\leq i\leq N) denotes the i-th character of S, and we define S_{N+1}=S_1, S_{N+2}=S_2, and A_{N+1}=A_1. Perform one of the following operations: Choose an integer i with 1\leq i\leq N such that S_i= A, S_{i+1}= R, and S_{i+2}= C, and replace each of A_i and A_{i+1} with 1. Choose an integer i with 1\leq i\leq N such that S_{i+2}= A, S_{i+1}= R, and S_i= C, and replace each of A_i and A_{i+1} with 1. Not specified; if both operations are simultaneously applicable for some i, either may be chosen (they don't conflict, since both only ever set A_i and A_{i+1} to 1). Determine whether there exists a good string. Input The input is given from Standard Input in the following format: N A_1 A_2 \dots A_N Output If there exists a good string, print Yes; otherwise, print No. The judge is case-insensitive; for example, if the correct answer is Yes, outputs such as yes, YES, or yEs will also be accepted. Constraints - 3\leq N\leq 200000 - A_i\in \lbrace 0,1 \rbrace (1\leq i\leq N) - All input values are integers.
